lead: The engine needs a known mass of air for every stroke because fuel quantity is set from air charge. A mass air flow (MAF) sensor measures this mass directly; a vane meter measures air volume flow and needs a density correction. A manifold absolute pressure (MAP) sensor measures intake pressure, and the ECU computes mass from pressure, speed, displacement and temperature. These sensors sit in the intake path and feed the engine control unit (ECU). They are used in petrol and diesel fuel control, turbo boost control, exhaust gas recirculation and diagnostics. Get the air charge wrong and the mixture, torque and emissions all drift.
prereq: You need: sensor basics and signal conditioning (bridges and conditioning), the ideal gas law p = ρRT and engine displacement; how the ECU turns air mass into a fuel pulse is in the electronic fuel control topic of electronic engine control.

blocks.text: Manifold absolute pressure (MAP) is the absolute pressure inside the intake manifold after the throttle, measured in kPa. At idle the throttle is nearly closed, so MAP may be 20–40 kPa. At wide-open throttle in a naturally aspirated engine it rises toward barometric pressure. Barometric pressure is local atmospheric pressure, about 100 kPa at sea level and lower at altitude. With ignition on and engine off, MAP equals barometric pressure, which lets the ECU check the sensor and learn altitude.

A MAP sensor turns pressure into voltage. In a strain-gauge MAP sensor, a diaphragm bends under pressure. Foil or diffused strain gauges are bonded to it, and their resistance changes with strain. The gauges form a Wheatstone bridge. The bridge output is small, so signal conditioning amplifies and filters it.
V<sub>o</sub> is bridge output in V; V<sub>ex</sub> is excitation voltage in V; R is gauge resistance in Ω; ΔR is its change in Ω. This is the small-change quarter-bridge result.

A capacitive MAP sensor uses the diaphragm as one plate of a capacitor. Pressure moves the diaphragm, changes the gap and changes capacitance; an oscillator and detector convert this to voltage. A piezoresistive MAP sensor uses resistors diffused into a silicon diaphragm. Pressure bends the silicon and changes resistance. The bridge and signal conditioning sit inside the sensor. A typical transfer is 0.5 V at 20 kPa and 4.5 V at 100 kPa. The ECU uses a stored table for accuracy. Some syllabi call this a strain gauge pressure sensor.

An air flow meter measures the air entering the engine. The oldest is the vane meter: a spring-loaded flap is pushed by air, and a potentiometer reports flap angle. It is simple but causes pressure loss and wears.

Hot-wire and hot-film meters keep a heated element at a fixed temperature above the incoming air. Moving air cools the element. The circuit increases current to hold the temperature, and that current measures mass flow. The element sits in a Wheatstone bridge. The bridge balances when the heated element resistance, and hence temperature, is fixed. After shutdown, a burn-off pulse heats the wire to around 1000 °C for about a second to burn off dirt. This keeps calibration stable. Hot-film sensors use a flat film and are more rugged; hot-wire sensors use a thin platinum wire and respond faster. Intake air temperature (IAT) is used to correct density and bridge drift.

A Karman vortex meter places a bluff body in the air stream. Vortices shed alternately downstream. The shedding frequency f is proportional to air velocity v: f = St × v ÷ d. Here f is frequency in Hz, St is the dimensionless Strouhal number (about 0.2), v is velocity in m/s, and d is bluff body width in m. A pressure or ultrasonic sensor counts vortices. Frequency gives velocity; density from pressure and temperature is needed for mass flow. These meters have no moving parts and low pressure loss.

The speed-density method uses MAP, engine speed, displacement, volumetric efficiency and intake temperature. Volumetric efficiency η<sub>v</sub> is the actual air volume trapped per intake stroke divided by the displaced volume, referenced to manifold conditions. It is dimensionless. With this reference it is typically 0.8–1.0 for naturally aspirated engines and stays near 1 for turbocharged engines. I<sub>f</sub> VE is referenced to ambient pressure instead, a boosted engine can exceed 1.

ṁ<sub>air</sub> is air mass flow in kg/s; P<sub>man</sub> is MAP in Pa absolute; V<sub>d</sub> is total engine displacement in m³; N is engine speed in rev/s; R is 287 J/(kg·K) for air; T is intake air temperature in K; η<sub>v</sub> is volumetric efficiency. The factor N/2 appears because a four-stroke engine has one intake stroke per two revolutions.

The mass-air method uses a MAF sensor and measures mass flow directly. It needs no volumetric efficiency table, so it handles altitude, intake leaks and engine wear better. It costs more, and the hot element can be contaminated. The speed-density method is cheaper and uses a MAP sensor, but it depends on the VE table and correct IAT and barometric pressure. Many ECUs use MAF for steady operation and MAP for transient correction and diagnostics.

examples.question: A 1.6 L four-stroke petrol engine runs at 3000 rpm. MAP is 60 kPa absolute and intake air temperature is 300 K. Volumetric efficiency is 0.90. Take R = 287 J/(kg·K). Estimate the air mass flow in kg/s and g/s.
steps: For a four-stroke engine, the number of engine cycles per second = N ÷ 2 = 50 ÷ 2 = 25 s⁻¹.
Convert pressure: P<sub>man</sub> = 60 kPa = 60,000 Pa absolute.
Air density at manifold conditions: ρ = P<sub>man</sub> ÷ (R × T) = 60,000 ÷ (287 × 300) = 0.6969 kg/m³.
Ideal air mass inducted per engine cycle (all cylinders together): ρ × V<sub>d</sub> = 0.6969 × 0.0016 = 0.001115 kg.
Actual air mass per engine cycle: η<sub>v</sub> × 0.001115 = 0.90 × 0.001115 = 0.0010035 kg.
Convert to g/s: 0.02509 × 1000 = 25.09 g/s, about 25.1 g/s.
examples.answer: The estimated air mass flow is 0.0251 kg/s, which is 25.1 g/s.
examples.check:
P_man = 60000.0
V_d = 0.0016
N = 3000.0 / 60.0
eta_v = 0.90
T = 300.0
R = 287.0
mdot = eta_v * P_man * V_d * (N / 2.0) / (R * T)
print(round(mdot, 4))
print(round(mdot * 1000.0, 1))

examples.question: A Karman vortex air flow meter has a bluff body 20 mm wide in a 50 mm diameter intake duct. The ECU counts 200 vortices per second. Take the Strouhal number as 0.20, the intake air at 100 kPa and 300 K, and R = 287 J/(kg·K). Find the air velocity, the volume flow and the mass flow in g/s.
steps: Velocity from the shedding law f = St × v ÷ d: v = f × d ÷ St = 200 × 0.020 ÷ 0.20 = 20.0 m/s.
Duct area: A = π d² ÷ 4 = π × 0.050² ÷ 4 = 0.001963 m².
Check: the vortex count gives volume flow only; the 1.161 kg/m³ came from the pressure and temperature sensors, so a wrong intake air temperature reading gives a wrong mass.
examples.answer: v = 20.0 m/s, Q = 0.0393 m³/s and ṁ = 45.6 g/s; the meter needs pressure and temperature to turn its volume reading into mass.

traps: Using rpm directly in the speed-density formula. Convert to rev/s and remember the N/2 factor for a four-stroke engine.
Using gauge pressure instead of absolute pressure. MAP and P<sub>man</sub> must be absolute, and in Pa inside the formula.
Treating MAF and MAP as interchangeable. MAF gives mass flow directly; MAP needs speed, displacement, volumetric efficiency and temperature.
Thinking Karman vortex frequency alone gives mass flow. Frequency gives velocity; density correction is needed for mass.
Reading burn-off current as a flow signal. Burn-off is a cleaning pulse after shutdown, not a measurement phase.

quiz.q: What does MAP stand for, and in what units is it usually given?
quiz.a: Manifold absolute pressure; usually kPa absolute.

quiz.q: Why does a hot-wire MAF need a burn-off cycle?
quiz.a: To burn off dirt and oil so the wire's heat transfer and calibration stay stable.

quiz.q: A 2.0 L four-stroke engine at 2400 rpm has MAP 50 kPa absolute, η<sub>v</sub> = 0.85 and intake temperature 300 K. Take R = 287 J/(kg·K). Estimate air mass flow in kg/s and g/s.
A car with speed-density fuel control climbs to high altitude. Barometric pressure falls. Explain why the ECU still needs barometric pressure information and what can go wrong without it.
quiz.a: MAP is absolute, so the density term falls with pressure. Barometric pressure is needed to select the correct volumetric-efficiency table, check key-on MAP and set diagnostic limits. Without it, fuel and limits can be wrong, giving a rich mixture or false faults.

quiz.q: State the Karman vortex frequency relation and define each symbol.
quiz.a: f = St × v ÷ d. f is vortex frequency in Hz; St is the dimensionless Strouhal number; v is air velocity in m/s; d is bluff body width in m.

quiz.q: A MAP sensor has transfer V = 0.05 × P<sub>kPa</sub> − 0.5. What pressure does 3.0 V indicate?

quiz.a: Actual air volume trapped per intake stroke divided by displaced volume, referenced to manifold conditions; dimensionless. With that reference it is typically 0.8–1.0 naturally aspirated and near 1 for turbocharged; referenced to ambient, a boosted engine can exceed 1.

beyond: Not for the exam. Modern engine management often combines a digital MAF with integrated IAT and a MAP sensor, then estimates air charge in a model that also uses throttle and cam timing. Research looks at robust hot-film contamination detection and model-based observers for transient air charge. Newer curricula add intake oxygen sensors and low-pressure EGR pressure sensors. Search for air charge estimation, MAF transfer function and speed-density volumetric efficiency table.
